passage:
I've shared a room with Suraj for two years, so I know his style. He never books the train until the night before, never picks between two electives until the last hour, and somehow it usually works. When our college fest lost its sound vendor on the morning of the event, Suraj was the one who borrowed speakers from the dance society and rewired the stage in an hour. Nobody else could switch that fast. Our group report was another story. He kept saying, "I'll slot it in when I see the week." On the Friday it was due, his section was blank. I can't say if he was worried; he looked calm. Afterwards, though, he asked me to put a Wednesday reminder on the shared calendar for every deadline. Since then, his part has come in on Wednesdays.
Kunal

qa.q: What did Suraj borrow when the fest lost its sound vendor?
qa.a: He borrowed speakers from the dance society.

qa.q: Why might Suraj have asked for a Wednesday reminder after the blank section?
qa.a: He seems to have realised that his wait-and-see style needs a fixed anchor for shared deadlines, even though he looked calm.

qa.q: What choice did Suraj make after the report went wrong, and how did it help?
qa.a: He asked Kunal for a Wednesday reminder on every deadline, and since then his part has come in on time.

qa.q: What is it like for Kunal and the group when Suraj's section is blank on the due date?
qa.a: They are left let down and scrambling on shared work, even though they rely on his quick thinking when plans collapse.

grounding: A roommate describes a young man who decides late and adapts brilliantly, but needs a fixed reminder to meet shared deadlines.

passage:
Sunday. Chaitanya sent the trek plan to the group: homestay deposits due by Wednesday. Zubin replied with a thumbs-up and "Let's see how the week goes."
Wednesday. The deposit link closed at midnight. Zubin had spent the evening helping his cousin move flats on a whim, and forgot. Chaitanya paid his share, jaw tight.
Saturday. At the bus stand the early bus was cancelled. While the others argued, Zubin had already found a shared jeep and bargained seats for all six. On the ride up he handed Chaitanya the deposit money. "Next trip, give me the deadline and I'll put it in my phone that minute. The rest I'll keep loose." Chaitanya laughed. "Deal. You're in charge of disasters."

qa.q: What did Zubin find when the early bus was cancelled?
qa.a: He found a shared jeep and bargained seats for all six.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's tight jaw on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Chaitanya felt annoyed and strained at having to cover Zubin's forgotten deposit.

qa.q: What choice did Zubin make on the ride up, and why does it suit his style?
qa.a: He paid back the deposit and promised to set deadlines in his phone at once while keeping the rest loose, anchoring only what others depend on.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Zubin differently by Saturday?
qa.a: Chaitanya sees both sides: someone who needs backing up on deadlines, and the one who rescues the trip when plans fall apart.

grounding: Over one week, a spontaneous young man misses a shared deadline, then shines when plans change and sets himself one fixed anchor.

passage:
Monday. Hafsa wanted to split the street-play project into roles and dates. 'Let's see how it flows,' Nitin said. 'We'll know what's needed when it's needed.'
Thursday. An hour before the show, the college moved it from the open lawn to a narrow corridor. Everyone panicked except Nitin. He re-blocked every scene in forty minutes, turned the corridor into a railway platform, and the crowd loved it.
The next Monday. The written report was due at five. At four, Hafsa asked for Nitin's section. He hadn't started. 'You said we'd know what's needed,' she said, voice tight. 'This was needed.' Nitin's ears burned. He wrote until six, apologised to the professor for the delay, and that night set three dates in his phone with alarms: rehearsal, report, show. 'Everything else,' he told Hafsa, 'I'll still wing.'

qa.q: Where did the college move the show on Thursday?
qa.a: From the open lawn to a narrow corridor.

qa.q: What did Nitin feel when Hafsa said 'This was needed'?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and guilty, his ears burning, seeing that his 'see how it flows' had left her waiting.

qa.q: What anchors did Nitin set, and why do they suit his style?
qa.a: Three dates with alarms for rehearsal, report and show; they fix the shared commitments while leaving him free to adapt everything else.

qa.q: How did Hafsa experience Nitin's style across those two weeks?
qa.a: She saw it rescue the show on Thursday, then felt let down and tense when the report deadline came without his part.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose flexible, decide-late style shines when plans change but fails a shared deadline until he sets deliberate anchors.

passage: Kishore, you ask why I write only three kinds of things in ink on my calendar. At your age I never booked anything. Trains, jobs, plans, I decided on the platform. And I was good at it: when a shoot in Hampi was cancelled, I found a village fair in two hours and came back with better photos than anyone. Editors loved me for it. Then my friend Latha asked me to photograph her wedding. I said yes, of course, and wrote it nowhere. That week a magazine offered me Ladakh. I went. I remembered on the plane. Latha didn't speak to me for two years. After that I kept my freedom for everything except three things: deadlines, promises, people. Those go in ink. Everything else, your Sarita Bua still decides on the platform.

qa.q: What did Sarita do when the Hampi shoot was cancelled?
qa.a: She found a village fair in two hours and came back with better photos than anyone.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt when she remembered the wedding on the plane?
qa.a: She probably felt a sinking guilt and shame, realising she had broken a promise to a friend.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed how Sarita worked afterwards?
qa.a: Deciding to put deadlines, promises and people in ink, while staying spontaneous about everything else.

qa.q: How was Latha affected by Sarita's choice to go to Ladakh?
qa.a: Latha lost her photographer on her wedding day, felt let down, and didn't speak to Sarita for two years.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a young adult whose spontaneous style works well with change but breaks a shared commitment, until she sets fixed anchors.

passage: The rain came down at noon on fest day, and the open lawn turned to mud. Sabina didn't blink. Within twenty minutes she had dragged their stall under the library stairwell, chalked RAIN SPECIAL: GINGER CHAI on a board, and sent Asif to call it through the corridors. By two there was a queue. 'You're a genius,' Asif said. At four the burner sputtered and died. The gas. On Friday Asif had asked her to book the refill, and she had said, 'I'll see how the day goes.' Now thirty people stood waiting with cups. Asif just looked at her. Sabina's cheeks went hot. That night, on the back of the chai board, she wrote three things that would never again be 'I'll see': gas, cash box, closing time. Everything else could stay open.

qa.q: What did Sabina chalk on the board?
qa.a: RAIN SPECIAL: GINGER CHAI.

qa.q: What does Sabina's cheeks going hot suggest?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and guilty, knowing her 'I'll see' about the gas had let Asif and the customers down.

qa.q: What is the point of the three things Sabina wrote down?
qa.a: They are anchors for shared commitments, so her flexibility stays for everything else while the essentials don't slip.

qa.q: What might Asif have felt when he just looked at her?
qa.a: Asif was probably frustrated and let down, having asked about the gas on Friday, even after praising her quick thinking.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose spontaneous style rescues a stall in the rain but lets a shared commitment slip, prompting fixed anchors.

passage: Tushar, twenty, never booked anything early. At his Bengaluru college, friends joked he decided lunch at the counter. But when the chief guest for the fest cancelled an hour before the opening, Tushar was the one who calmly rang an alumni band, rearranged the stage order and had the crowd singing in twenty minutes. Two weeks later, though, he forgot the group project deadline entirely. Sonali, his partner, was furious. "Your flexibility is great, but I can't be your calendar." Tushar felt embarrassed. That evening they agreed on two anchors: a shared calendar with alerts for every deadline, and a check-in every Monday at nine. He still decided lunch at the counter. But he never missed another submission.

qa.q: What did Tushar arrange when the chief guest cancelled?
qa.a: He rang an alumni band, rearranged the stage order and had the crowd singing in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when Sonali got angry about the deadline?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, realising his style had let her down.

qa.q: What anchors did they agree on, and why do they help?
qa.a: A shared calendar with deadline alerts and a Monday check-in, so Tushar's flexibility doesn't break shared commitments.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about carrying the deadlines alone?
qa.a: Sonali felt frustrated and angry, refusing to be Tushar's calendar.

grounding: Shows a young adult who adapts well in changing situations but needs deliberate anchors like shared calendars for deadlines and commitments.
